messages.subject: fmin = 0 when
parts:
Hi Yves et al., 

I'm running a simulation study in which I'm fitting misspecified models, so I expect things to go wrong. But I'm puzzled: in a huge number of cases (~90% of my replications), I get what appears to be perfect model fit (fmin = 0, so all other fit indices = 0, despite large model residuals; SRMR is typically big). These replications give a bunch of warning messages, but no errors. The model appears to converge and I get standard errors (though I also get heywood cases). 

I'm wondering why fmin would be 0. Any ideas? 

Is there ever a situation with real data when you would be able to interpret the results despite these warning messages? i.e., is this really a case of convergence failure? 

Thanks for your thoughts! 
Mijke

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: fmin = 0 when
parts:
Warning messages:
1: In lav_samplestats_from_moments(sample.cov = sample.cov, sample.mean = sample.mean,  :
  lavaan WARNING: sample covariance can not be inverted

Hi Mijke!  Do you know why covMat can't be inverted?  Have you looked at the determinant or eigen decomposition?

det(covMat)
eigen(covMat)

Was covMat produced directly, or indirectly via model parameters?  I wouldn't expect a covariance matrix calculated from real (complete) data to be uninvertible, but is covMat calculated from a sample?

Here's an example covariance matrix, and the model: 
> covMat
             m1        m2        m3        m4         Y          X
[1,] 1.00000000 0.8117067 0.8117067 0.8117067 0.3706815 0.04348156
[2,] 0.81170673 1.0000000 0.8117067 0.8117067 0.3706815 0.19893281
[3,] 0.81170673 0.8117067 1.0000000 0.8117067 0.3706815 0.35587069
[4,] 0.81170673 0.8117067 0.8117067 1.0000000 0.3706815 0.88444112
[5,] 0.37068154 0.3706815 0.3706815 0.3706815 1.0000000 0.16000000
[6,] 0.04348156 0.1989328 0.3558707 0.8844411 0.1600000 1.00000000

I don't know if there is an easy way to import this matrix output into R.  Could you use the unfortunately named dump() function?

dump("covMat", file = "")

That will print some R syntax to your console, which you can copy/paste in a message for anyone to easily import your data.  

Something that looks odd to me is that m1-m4 have uniform correlations (by implication, equal factor loadings on LM), but X has a wide variety of correlations with m1-m4.  So the single effect of X on LM might not allow for such differential indirect effects on LM's indicators.  The optimizer's balancing act is probably responsible for the Heywood cases, but I don't know whether it's related to fmin == 0.  The fact you get perfect fit and covMat can't be inverted makes me wonder whether there is linear dependence among some variables, or whether covMat is a possible correlation matrix.

Terry

messages.author: a2d9b83cabaa80ae
messages.subject: Re: fmin = 0 when
parts:
Hi Terry!

No, it's not a positive-definite matrix. It's population data from a model, and the data are not possible. Practically, this means I need to discount these conditions. I guess it's more of an academic question -- why, given a non-positive definite matrix, would lavaan apparently converge, give standard errors, and produce fmin = 0? 

(As you noted, the differential effect of X on m1-m4 is responsible for misfit -- this is (clearly) not the generating model and I don't expect it to fit well. But I expected errors, not an apparently perfectly fitting model). 

Best,
Mijke

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: fmin = 0 when
parts: I guess it's more of an academic question -- why, given a non-positive definite matrix, would lavaan apparently converge, give standard errors, and produce fmin = 0?

Good question.  I am surprised that lavaan proceeds to fit a model to NPD matrices -- although perhaps that is necessary to allow models to be fit when there are missing ordered data and we want to use pairwise deletion (which might yield a NPD polychoric matrix).

The SEs just mean that the information matrix can be inverted.  But it does seem suspicious that lavaan found a perfectly fitting solution, so I used your example data & model, and I found something curious:

covMat <- structure(c(1, 0.81170673, 0.81170673, 0.81170673, 0.37068154, 
                      0.04348156, 0.8117067, 1, 0.8117067, 0.8117067, 0.3706815, 0.1989328, 
                      0.8117067, 0.8117067, 1, 0.8117067, 0.3706815, 0.3558707, 0.8117067, 
                      0.8117067, 0.8117067, 1, 0.3706815, 0.8844411, 0.3706815, 0.3706815, 
                      0.3706815, 0.3706815, 1, 0.16, 0.04348156, 0.19893281, 0.35587069, 
                      0.88444112, 0.16, 1), .Dim = c(6L, 6L),
                    .Dimnames = list(c("m1","m2","m3","m4","Y","X"),
                                     c("m1","m2","m3","m4","Y","X")))
LVMod <- 'LM =~ m1 + m2 + m3 + m4

Y ~ LM
          LM ~ X'
fitLV <- sem(model = LVMod, sample.cov = covMat, sample.nobs = 100,
                  sample.cov.rescale = FALSE)

The observed (S) and model-implied (Sigma) covariance matrices DO differ, so the solution should not be perfectly fitting.

> (S <- lavInspect(fitLV, "sampstat")$cov)
m1    m2    m3    m4    Y     X

m1 1.000                              
m2 0.812 1.000                        
m3 0.812 0.812 1.000                  
m4 0.812 0.812 0.812 1.000            
Y  0.371 0.371 0.371 0.371 1.000      
X  0.043 0.199 0.356 0.884 0.160 1.000
> (Sigma <- lavInspect(fitLV, "sigma.hat"))
m1    m2    m3    m4    Y     X

m1 0.797                              
m2 0.509 0.797                        
m3 0.503 0.515 0.773                  
m4 0.612 0.628 0.620 0.718            
Y  0.209 0.214 0.211 0.257 0.735      
X  0.680 0.697 0.688 0.838 0.286 1.000

Because S cannot be inverted, it has a negative determinant, and log(det(S)) == NaN, so that should mean fmin == NaN.  But because X is treated as a fixed exogenous variable by default, its variance and covariances are not estimated parameters, so fmin is not calculated from the 6x6 matrix.  I assume it is calculated from the 5x5 submatrix (excluding row/column X), which as it turns out, is positive definite:

> fS <- S[-6,-6]
> fSigma <- Sigma[-6,-6]
> det(fS)
[1] 0.01926308

So it would be possible to calculate fmin from the reduced matrices.  But I don't that is what lavaan does because that quantity is also not zero:

> log(det(fSigma)) - log(det(fS)) + sum(diag(fS %*% solve(fSigma))) - nrow(fS)
[1] 1.42241

I am unsure exactly how fmin is calculated in the presence of fixed exogenous variables, but even after setting "fixed.x = FALSE" (in which case I would expect fmin == NaN because log(det(S)) == NaN), lavaan still returned fmin == 0.  So I am curious what Yves has to say about this situation.

Terry

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: fmin = 0 when
parts: > So I am curious what Yves has to say about this situation.

Well, interesting.

So, I am surprised too. Apparently, for some reason (my memory fails me
here), I tried to handle non-positive input matrices somehow. You can
see it in the file lav_samplestats_icov.R (in 0.5-20).

The intent was to apply ridging for the exogenous variables only, but
the actual implementation does ridging for all variables. If that fails
too, I use a generalized inverse, AND ... I set the log determinant to
log(.Machine$double.eps) (resulting in about -36.04365)

I guess the idea is then to find parameters which produce a
model-implied covariance matrix that is nearly-singular, which may still
be useful.

That might actually work ... unless you also allow for negative
variances (which lavaan does). This circumvents this logic and may
produce a value for the discrepancy measure which is negative, which
then will be cut off to zero... which is what we have here.

In any case, it seems clear that the current behavior is unwanted. I
still think ridging can be ok, but for exogenous variables only.

As for a direct workaround: check the input matrix first, before running
lavaan.

Yves.
